KEY MESSAGE 1...
The upper level ridge continues to build across the southeastern 
CONUS allowing for temperatures and humidity to build across the 
Great Lakes region through mid week. Low level flow will generally 
be out of the west to southwest into Friday morning that will be the 
main driver to advect in the warmer and moist air mass from the 
south. 850mb temperatures will begin to warm today to around 20-22C 
across the region and persist through Thursday. The warmer side of 
those temperatures will be across western Ohio with temperatures a 
few degrees cooler to the east. Regardless, high temperatures are 
expected to rise into the upper 80s to low 90s today then with more 
widespread 90s on Wednesday. Dew points will also climb into the 
upper 60s to low 70s. This will push heat indices up to the upper 
90s to low 100s with the higher end out west where the current heat 
advisory is issued. Additionally, there will be little relief 
overnight as lows will only drop down into the mid to low 70s. The 
advisory is currently valid starting this afternoon through 
Wednesday evening. As with normal summer heat, take precautions when 
outdoors and limit strenuous activities during peak heating periods. 

There is some uncertainty with how warm the eastern Ohio and 
northwestern Pennsylvania will get as rounds of precipitation is 
expected through Thursday. This will generally keep temperatures 
"down" a bit with the precipitation and consistent cloud coverage. 
Though, there maybe enough breaks in the precipitation to allow for 
temperatures to rise enough for heat indices to reach the upper 90s. 
Will have to watch how each system develops to see if an eastward 
expansion of the advisory will be necessary over the next couple of 
days. For Thursday, a low pressure system will be moving to the 
north, and will sweep a cold front through the region that day. 
There should be enough widespread precipitation during the day to 
keep temperatures down. The upper level ridge will begin to weaken 
across the region and temperatures will fall to be more seasonal 
this weekend. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...
Along the upper level ridge, a series of shortwaves are expected to 
move through the Great Lakes region beginning today through Thursday 
resulting in rounds of unsettled weather. A warm and moist air mass 
will be in place across the region with a large surface high to the 
south. Ample instability of around 2000 MLCAPE will be in place for 
much of the week with bulk shear vectors of around 35-40 knots. 
PWATs will also be elevated during this time period at 1.5-2.0", so 
any thunderstorms that move through will have the threat for heavy 
rain as well. 

The first of the shortwaves are expected to move into the region 
late tonight into early Wednesday morning. There's plenty of 
uncertainty regarding the timing and placement of thunderstorms as 
most CAMs disagree with each other. Any storms should follow the 
instability gradient which will be situated across northeastern 
Ohio, though how far west or east it sets up depends on if any 
precipitation forms today along the lake shore and limits the 
instability or if there is no development today and it builds east 
further. Timing is also an issue as some models have the feature 
moving into northeastern Ohio by 6Z Wednesday morning whereas other 
are a few hours later. Once the feature gets going up stream, there 
will be a better idea of the timing and placement as it moves into 
the region. There should be enough in place though that if storms do 
form, the would be a damaging wind threat with a secondary threat of 
large hail. 

There will be a break in the precipitation after this feature moves 
late Wednesday morning into the afternoon. Confidence is low, but 
some thunderstorms are possible Wednesday afternoon into the evening 
developing off a lake breeze or outflows from the mornings storms. 
Though the majority should remain dry throughout the day. The next 
round of thunderstorms are expected later Wednesday night into 
Thursday morning. A low pressure system will be moving north of the 
Great Lakes Wednesday night into Thursday and will sweep a cold 
front through the region on Thursday. The timing of the front is 
still fairly uncertain as it has shifted over the past few model 
runs and varies between models as well. If the front slows, then 
there may be enough time Thursday morning into the mid day to allow 
for a greater severe weather threat. Though, if it is on the quicker 
side, then the severe threat may be lower. Will need to monitor how 
this develops with the convection earlier in the day and timing of 
the front. 

For the remainder of Thursday into Friday, showers and thunderstorms 
are likely though should be more widespread with the front and with 
the surface high to the south retreating. Additionally, another 
shortwave is possible late Thursday into Friday that will provide 
enough support to keep scattered showers and thunderstorms
